passage: Mentor's note, Tuesday. Siddharth (Class 12) printed a topper's daily routine of sixteen hours from social media and pinned it above his desk. It began before dawn and ran until midnight, with almost no room for meals. He kept it for ten days. By day eight he was late to class; on day ten he slept through the morning and told me he had not opened a book since. He now studies perhaps an hour a day. The schedule had no place for his sleep, his slower pace in chemistry or the fact that he needs a break after lunch. I asked him to note when he naturally gets sleepy and how long he can focus before his mind drifts. We meet again on Thursday. — Ishita

qa.q: How many hours did the copied schedule contain?
What might Siddharth be feeling now?
qa.a: Discouraged and drained: after the burnout he has almost stopped studying.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do instead of copying a schedule, and why?
qa.a: Build a timetable from his own sleep, focus span and pace, since a routine that ignores these breaks quickly.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Ishita?
qa.a: Ishita sees a student who worked hard on something unsuited to him and lost a lot, and wants to help him find his own rhythm instead of scolding.

grounding: A student copies a topper's sixteen-hour timetable from social media, burns out in ten days and nearly stops studying.
